trinity-development.summary: From Christ’s command to baptize, the Church always named Father, Son and Spirit together. Wrong teachings forced her to say clearly what that means. The Son is of one being with the Father (Nicaea, 325). The Spirit is worshipped with them (Constantinople, 381). The faith stayed the same. The words grew sharper.

steps.0: Jesus commands baptism in one name that holds Father, Son and Spirit.
steps.1: Ignatius shows the threefold pattern was not a later habit.
steps.2: Justin reports the threefold name as the normal way to baptize.
steps.3: Irenaeus answers Gnostics who made up secret teachings.
steps.4: Nicaea answers Arius, who said the Son was a creature.
steps.5: The same creed names the error it rules out.
steps.6: Athanasius defends the Son and Spirit against later Arian arguments.
steps.7: Constantinople answers those who denied the Spirit is God.
steps.8: The Catechism sums it up: same teaching, stated more exactly.

objections: The council added a word, not a teaching. Scripture already says the Word was God. Arians accepted every Bible phrase while denying its plain sense. So the bishops chose a word they could not twist.
No. The Church teaches one divine nature, whole in each Person. The Persons differ only in how they relate to each other.
The decision of 381 made clear what was already believed. The Spirit was named with Father and Son in baptism from the start.

christ-natures-development.summary: The apostles said the Word became flesh. Each century raised a new question. Is the Son truly God? Is Christ one person? Are both natures real and not mixed? Does he have a human will? The Church answered each time by guarding the same Gospel. She added nothing new.

steps.0: The starting point: the Word became flesh and lived among us.
steps.1: Athanasius says the Saviour had to be both God and man.
steps.2: Nicaea says the Son is true God, of one being with the Father.
steps.3: Cyril answers a view that seemed to split the Word and the man Jesus.
steps.4: Leo answers a view that swallowed Christ’s humanity into his divinity.
steps.5: Chalcedon says one Christ, perfect God and perfect man.
steps.6: Constantinople II says the one Person is the eternal Word.
steps.7: Constantinople III says Christ has a human will and a divine will.
steps.8: The Catechism: nothing taken from his divinity, nothing from his humanity.

objections: The councils borrowed words to defend what Scripture already says. He was in the form of God and took the form of a servant. The words are a fence around that truth.
No. Constantinople III says each nature does what is proper to it, with no division. One Person wills and acts in both ways.
They were about salvation. If Christ were not truly God, he could not join us to God. If he were not truly man, he could not redeem human nature.

mary-development.summary: Luke calls Mary “highly favored”, which the Latin tradition renders “full of grace”. She is the mother of the Lord. Irenaeus saw her obedience as the answer to Eve’s disobedience. Ephesus called her Theotokos to protect the truth about Christ. Later thought on “full of grace” led Pius IX to define the Immaculate Conception.

steps.0: The angel greets Mary with a title of grace.
steps.1: Irenaeus answers Gnostics who said Christ only passed through Mary.
steps.2: Irenaeus sets Mary’s obedience beside Eve’s disobedience.
steps.3: Ephesus answers an objection to calling Mary Theotokos.
steps.4: Constantinople II names her ever-virgin Mother of God.
steps.5: John of Damascus says Mother of God is strictly true.
steps.6: Pius IX defines that Mary was kept from sin from the start, by Christ’s merits.
steps.7: The Catechism says her holiness comes wholly from Christ.

objections: It appears in the second century in Irenaeus, who received the faith from apostolic churches. It rests on Luke’s account of Mary’s answer to the angel.
The title was set to protect Christ’s identity. Cyril says the Word’s divinity did not begin in Mary. She is mother of the Person.
It is not stated in those words. The Church reads Luke’s “highly favored” with the Eastern title All-Holy. She holds it was part of the faith and was defined in 1854. It was debated for a long time.

real-presence-development.summary: Paul and John say the bread and cup are Christ’s body and blood. The early Fathers speak the same way. Later, some reduced it to a mere sign. The Church answered, at Lateran IV and Trent, that Christ is truly, really and wholly present.

steps.0: Paul hands on the words “This is my body” at the Last Supper.
steps.1: Jesus says his flesh is food indeed.
steps.2: Ignatius calls the bread of God the flesh of Christ.
steps.3: Irenaeus answers Gnostics who despised the body.
steps.4: Cyril tells the newly baptized to trust the Lord’s word.
steps.5: Ambrose points to the Incarnation, which also went beyond nature.
steps.6: Augustine reads the Psalms in the light of the Supper.
steps.7: Trent answers those who called the Eucharist only a sign.
steps.8: The Catechism: the presence is real in the fullest sense, the whole Christ.

objections: They do use sign language. They never say Christ is absent. Augustine says faith is needed. Trent rejects the claim that Christ is present only in a sign.
The Fathers face this same question. They say the senses tell us the look, and faith rests on Christ’s word. Ambrose and Cyril point to the Lord’s power to change things.
The word is later. The belief is not. The Fathers already speak of change. The word was chosen to name that change exactly.

canon-development.summary: From the start the Church read Scripture as inspired. The four Gospels were recognised early. For other books, she tested what was read in the churches and what came from the apostles. Some places differed for a time. Councils at Hippo and Carthage listed the books. Trent defined the list.

steps.0: Paul speaks of Scripture as God-breathed.
steps.1: Irenaeus defends the four Gospels against groups with their own.
steps.2: Origen says only the four Gospels were beyond dispute.
steps.3: Eusebius sorts the books into agreed and disputed.
steps.4: Cyril gives new Christians a list of what the Church reads.
steps.5: Augustine gives a rule for when churches differ.
steps.6: Trent lists the full canon after reformers set some books aside.
steps.7: Vatican I: the books are canonical because God is their author.
steps.8: The Catechism: the Church finds the canon through apostolic Tradition.

objections: Trent defined the list. The books were in use long before. Augustine counted Tobit, Judith and Maccabees in the late 300s. Some Fathers hesitated, which is why a clear decision was needed.
The Church recognises Scripture. She does not make it inspired. The books are canonical because God is their author.
No world-wide council fixed it early. But regional councils at Hippo and Carthage listed the books. Pope Innocent I sent a matching list in 405.

icons-development.summary: Israel was forbidden to worship images. Yet God commanded sacred figures in the tabernacle. When God became visible in the Incarnation, Christians painted Christ. Some then attacked images. John of Damascus and the Second Council of Nicaea said the honour given to an image passes to the person it shows.

steps.0: God forbids images made to be worshipped as gods.
steps.1: God orders carved cherubim in the tent.
steps.2: The Word became flesh and was seen.
steps.3: John of Damascus says the invisible God cannot be copied, so the image shows Christ in the flesh.
steps.4: John separates honouring an object from honouring the one it shows.
steps.5: Some leaders at Hieria said images go against the Incarnation. The Church did not accept it.
steps.6: Nicaea II says images belong to a tradition tied to the Incarnation.
steps.7: Nicaea II separates honour from worship, which is for God alone.
steps.8: The Catechism: honour goes to the person shown.

objections: The commandment forbids images made to be worshipped as gods. Scripture also commands carved cherubim. Nicaea II separates honour from worship.
There is early evidence of Christian images, such as catacomb paintings. Some early Christians opposed them. The Fathers at Nicaea II judged that images fit the Incarnation.
Christ is the visible image of the invisible God. The Word took a human body, so he can be seen and painted. Denying this would make the Incarnation only an appearance.

papal-primacy-development.summary: Christ gave Simon a special place among the apostles. In the first century, the Church of Rome already acts with unusual weight. In the second century she is spoken of that way. How far her authority reaches was argued for centuries. Vatican I defined the pope’s primacy in 1870, and also said the bishops keep their own power.

steps.0: A promise to one man, Simon, who is renamed and given the keys.
steps.1: Christ prays for Simon and gives him the task of strengthening the others.
steps.2: Rome writes to Corinth to settle a quarrel there.
steps.3: Ignatius uses special words for the Church at Rome.
steps.4: Irenaeus points to Rome as a test of the apostles’ faith.
steps.5: In a dispute with Rome, Cyprian roots unity in Peter.
steps.6: At Ephesus the pope’s helper states Peter’s role, and the council accepts it.
steps.7: Leo explains why he as bishop of Rome speaks for the whole Church.
steps.8: At Chalcedon the bishops welcome Leo’s Tome.
steps.9: Vatican I answers views that said the pope’s primacy was only honour.
steps.10: The Catechism: the pope is the visible source of unity.

objections: Cyprian is a true witness that the question was argued. He opposed Pope Stephen over rebaptism. But he also held that Peter was chosen first.
The early texts do not speak the language of 1870. The Church admits the teaching became clearer over time. The council claimed no new revelation. It used the same Gospel texts and the Fathers.
No. Vatican I says the opposite. The pope’s power does not harm the bishops’ own power. It supports it.

original-sin-development.summary: Scripture links sin and death in the human story to Adam. The Fathers read it that way. Pelagius said Adam only gave a bad example. Augustine, the African councils and Orange said Adam’s sin is passed on by birth, not by copying. Trent set the limits.

steps.0: The psalm speaks of sinfulness going back to a person’s beginning.
steps.1: Paul sets one man’s fall beside one man’s obedience.
steps.2: Irenaeus says all are bound up with Adam, and Christ renews them.
steps.3: Augustine explains why babies are baptized.
steps.4: Cœlestius would baptize babies but denied sin is passed on.
steps.5: Trent answers Reformers who said nature itself is corrupt.
steps.6: Trent says what stays in the baptized is a pull toward sin to struggle against.
steps.7: The Catechism: original sin is a state we are born into. Nature is wounded.

objections: The Church does not teach that anyone is personally guilty of Adam’s act. The Catechism says original sin is contracted, not committed. It is a loss of holiness.
That was the Pelagian reading. Augustine said that then Abel, not Christ, would head the righteous. If sin were only copying, Paul’s contrast would make no sense.
The Church said nature is wounded, not destroyed. Free will and real goodness stay. She steers between two extremes.

grace-development.summary: Paul says we have nothing we did not receive. God works in us to will and to do. Pelagius said we can keep the commands by our own will. Augustine said even the start of good is God’s gift, while free will is kept. Trent answered the Reformers with the same balance.

steps.0: Whatever is good in a person has been received.
steps.1: Salvation is by grace through faith. It is a gift.
steps.2: Paul says to work out our salvation. God works in us.
steps.3: Augustine says grace heals the will.
steps.4: Pelagius says nature is enough. Grace is only an extra help.
steps.5: Augustine holds both: grace is real, and free will is real.
steps.6: Trent answers those who said the will is only passive.
steps.7: Trent also rejects the Pelagian view. Even the first step of faith needs the Spirit.
steps.8: The Catechism quotes Augustine: God begins the work and finishes it.

objections: We are called to work, but Paul roots that work in God. The same passage says God works in you. Grace comes first. Our free yes is a response.
The Council of Trent rejected that conclusion. Grace does not override the will. It moves it to say yes freely.
The Catechism says the opposite. No one can merit the first grace. All later merit is itself a gift of God.

purgatory-development.summary: Praying for the dead is in Scripture and in the earliest Christian practice. The Fathers speak of a cleansing fire. Augustine said it is possible that some pass through such a fire, and left the question open. He was firm that the prayers and offerings of the Church help the dead.

steps.0: Judas Maccabeus offers a sacrifice for fallen soldiers.
steps.1: Paul’s image of a testing fire led later writers to think of cleansing after death.
steps.2: Cyprian shows that prayer for the dead was regular enough to be withheld as a penalty.
steps.3: Monica asks to be remembered at the altar.
steps.4: Augustine is careful about what 1 Corinthians 3 means.
steps.5: Augustine is firm that the Eucharist and alms help the dead.
steps.6: Trent defines the teaching and warns against excess.
steps.7: The Catechism: purgatory is a completion of holiness, not a second chance.

objections: The Catholic canon includes 2 Maccabees. The early practice of offering the Eucharist for the dead does not rest on that book alone. What came later is the exact vocabulary.

Augustine hesitated about how to understand a cleansing fire. He did not hesitate about the help the living can give the dead. Trent defines only that there is a purgatory and that the prayers of the faithful help.
No. The Catechism says punishment here is not revenge. It is the result of being attached to created things. Trent told bishops to forbid anything that smells of greed.

baptism-development.summary: Christ commanded baptism and linked it to new birth and forgiveness. From the start the Church baptized with water in the name of the Trinity. Arguments came: is it necessary, should babies be baptized, does baptism by heretics count? The Church answered step by step.

steps.0: The risen Christ gives the rite and the words.
steps.1: Christ ties entering the Kingdom to new birth of water and Spirit.
steps.2: Peter joins repentance, baptism, forgiveness and the Spirit.
steps.3: Justin describes a plain washing in the name of the Trinity.
steps.4: Tertullian defends baptism against those who called it too simple.
steps.5: A council of bishops says an infant need not wait until the eighth day.
steps.6: Cyprian’s bishops held that baptism by heretics did not count.
steps.7: Augustine says the sacrament belongs to Christ, so it is not repeated.
steps.8: Trent states what the earlier councils held.
steps.9: The Catechism: baptism is necessary, but God is not limited to it.

objections: Tertullian’s advice shows that infants were already baptized in his day. The African council wrote that none should be refused. The Church baptizes infants in the faith of the Church.

Cyprian held a view that was not yet settled. He said each bishop was free to follow his own judgment while keeping unity. The Church later followed Rome and Augustine, who said Christ is the true giver of baptism.
Baptism is the usual way, not the only one. A catechumen who dies is sure of salvation by desire. For babies who die unbaptized, the Church trusts God’s mercy.

confession-development.summary: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to hold back sins. The Church has used it from the beginning. The form changed from public penance to private confession. After persecution, bishops like Cyprian asked for confession and a return to the Church.

steps.0: The risen Christ sends the apostles and gives them power over sins.
steps.1: Early Christians practised confessing sins within the community.
steps.2: Ignatius ties repentance to returning to the Church’s unity.
steps.3: Tertullian describes a second repentance for sins after baptism.
steps.4: Cyprian lets the dying confess and be restored.
steps.5: Cyprian insists on confession and making amends.
steps.6: The Catechism: public penance for grave sins slowly became private confession.
steps.7: Trent says serious sins must be confessed to a priest.

objections: The Church agrees only God forgives. Jesus gave this power to men to use in his name. The priest is the servant. God is the one who forgives.

The Church admits the form changed. Public penance was the early way for grave sins. Private confession spread later. But the power to forgive, the need to confess and the priest’s role were already there.
The Church does not set 1 John aside. God forgives the sorry person. Christ chose to give that through the apostles and their successors.
